In my opinion, relative to a Hobbes-esque “state of anarchy,” states provide both the leaders and members with economic and evolutionary advantages. The advantages for the leaders are obvious, but the non-leaders of the state also reap a few (relative) advantages. The main service a state provides is a system of enforcement. To make any sort of long-term economic agreement, you have to feel confident that the other person won't violate the agreement. Historically, states have served as the enforcer of these sorts of agreements. Long-term economic agreements are what builds any sort of civilization. The state may not be (I believe it is not) the best possible system of enforcement of economic agreements (or contracts), but it is significantly better than nothing. 

States also provide a system of conflict resolution. Conflicts are almost always bad for both people involved, even if you win, you can be seriously injured. People who engage in less conflict are more likely to survive, so people who submit to a state have had an evolutionary advantage. 

I think it is important to acknowledge the important role that governments have played historically. That doesn't mean that governments are moral or necessary, it just means that governments do provide benefits to the people under it.

I think this is true -- the idea that there are benefits to governmental systems relative to chaos. However, better is not necessarily optimal, nor, as you've stated, moral or desirable.

Governments are an outdated solution to an age old issue. There is a better solution, IMO, but unfortunately there are a lot of barriers.

From what do you think this stability arises? To get where I'm going with this, consider how the outcome of one threat influences the outcome of the next threat.

I think it's stable because humans generally avoid stirring up too much trouble and as long as they're left alone to what they see as a reasonable degree, they're not willing to risk their families and their carefully ordered lives to overthrow a tyrant, they're much more likely to accept them as a fact of life.

As an example of this, in most revolutions, less than a tenth of the population participates.

Regrettably I don't know enough game theory to put my ideas on a more sound basis but I'll give this response a shot using plain language. The mutually reinforcing underpinnings of states as I understand them:

  • Organized military
  • Ability to deficit spend
  • Psychology of tribalism

Organized military: Having the ability to conscript thousands of people who will kill on command without having to compensate them for their efforts is very advantageous. For example active duty soldiers in the US get a ridiculously low hourly wage, way worse than the 'abused' chinese laborers. If there's a large unorganized territory with fractured alliances it's susceptible to being taken over by a single determined adversary. There are many historical examples implying this fact. Often many small city states which in aggregate are much stronger than the invader state nevertheless get conquered one by one because they do not coordinate with each other.

Ability to deficit spend: A state can run massively unprofitable "investments" for decades to accomplish its goals. A good example is the Cold War where two states had (and both still do to a large extent) massive biological, chemical, nuclear and space war programs that are massively unprofitable. It would be exceedingly hard to find Venture Capital for these types of projects. If you did find VCs for such projects I think the pitch would be "How would you like to be on the ruling council of a newly formed state?"

Psychology of Tribalism: As you know nationalism (aka tribalism) is a major source of legitimacy for states. This is not so much a brainwashing thing (although there is a lot of that) it's a human thing. People like feeling that they are a part of something bigger than themselves. Most people don't have this type of mass irrational loyalty in other contexts. The second most fanatic cause that people follow at scale are professional sport teams. I doubt the vast majority of people would risk conscription/death to see their basketball/soccer/football team succeed.

For the sake of brevity I decided omit historical examples or go too deeply in how these areas mutually reinforce each other.

What's interesting is what would happen to the state structure in the absence of external threats, but I don't think that's ever happened in human history.

Some number of people lust for power over others.

This has, in fact, been demonstrated in studies. I'd have to search to find it and I can't be arsed to do that right now, but researchers isolated groups of children and left them on their own and observed them surreptitiously. In all cases, something approximating 6% (IIRC) of the children would separate themselves out from the rest and take charge.

So in whatever group of people you might have, you'll have something approximating 6% of them who will seek to control the rest.

And that's really all it takes. Everything beyond that is trivia - the justifications for putting them in charge, the manner in which they'll purportedly be appointed to their positions, the constraints that will purportedly be placed upon them and so on - that's all just detail, and can be, and is, whatever serves to provide that 6% with the power they desire.

And of course, all of that is helped along immensely by the fact that there's another probably fairly standard percentage of the people who don't necessarily want power themselves, but who enjoy seeing it exercised against whoever they've chosen to be offended by, and another probably fairly standard percentage of people who want only to submit to someone else's power. Then there's a fairly large group that doesn't want to have to think about any of that crap and just keep their heads down. And all of those people, by action or inaction, enable those who lust for power.

The state, as a concept, is actually a relatively recent innovation. Before that was the divine right of kings, but it was really just the same thing - a specious justification for the establishment of a power structure for the benefit of those who lust for power.
